item.title: Association of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome Radiographic Findings Identified by Machine Learning and Outcomes of Patients Receiving Invasive Mechanical Ventilation
item.description:
Objectives: To determine whether predictions from a deep learning model that identifies acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) findings on chest radiographs (CXRs) can also predict clinical outcomes beyond traditional indicators of hypoxemia and illness severity.

Design: Retrospective cohort study.

Setting: Single academic medical center.

Intervention: None.

Patients: Adult patients with CXRs performed at the time of invasive mechanical ventilation initiation.

Methods and main results: We applied a deep learning model that was previously trained to identify bilateral airspace opacities consistent with ARDS to CXRs of 6591 patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation. The resulting ARDS-CXR scores were evaluated for their ability to discriminate risk of 28-day mortality and their association with 28-day mortality and time to extubation after adjusting for a patient's Pao2/Fio2 or Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation-IV. The median ARDS-CXR score was -2.09, corresponding to an ARDS probability of 15%, and 1089 (17%) patients had a positive score, corresponding to an ARDS probability above 50%. Twenty-eight-day mortality was 35.1% among patients with a positive score and 13.5% among patients with a negative score. ARDS-CXR scores below the ARDS threshold also stratified risk, with mortality increasing from 12.8% at a score of -2 to 19.9% at -1 and 27.5% at 0. The ARDS-CXR score area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC) curve was 0.68 (95% CI, 0.66-0.70) for predicting 28-day mortality, whereas the Pao2/Fio2 AUROC was 0.64 (95% CI, 0.62-0.66). After adjusting for either the patient's Pao2/Fio2 or Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation-IV, a 1-point increase in the ARDS-CXR score was significantly associated with higher 28-day mortality or prolonged time to extubation.

Conclusions: A deep learning-derived ARDS-CXR score quantifying radiographic findings of ARDS independently predicted mortality and ventilator outcomes beyond hypoxemia and illness severity. Algorithmically derived markers of lung injury severity from chest imaging could be used to support clinical care decisions, predictive enrichment in research studies, or incorporated into a future ARDS definition.

Zhong Y, Nuppnau M, Farzaneh N, Ansari S, Sjoding MW

item.title: Brachial-to-Radial Pressure Gradient in Critically Ill Patients Treated With Vasoactive Agents: A Prospective Observational Study
item.description:
Objectives: To determine the incidence of a significant noninvasive brachial-to-radial arterial pressure gradient (NIBR-APG) and its clinical associations in critically ill patients receiving vasoactive agents.

Design: Prospective, multicenter, observational study.

Setting: Thirteen ICUs in Poland.

Patients: Adult ICU patients with radial arterial catheters receiving vasoactive agents hospitalized between April 2025 and July 2025.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: Invasive radial mean arterial pressure (MAP) and noninvasive brachial MAP were measured twice and averaged. A NIBR-APG greater than 11 mm Hg was predefined as clinically significant. Baseline characteristics, hemodynamic variables, and outcomes were recorded. Among 303 patients, 49.5% were surgical admissions and 33.3% had septic shock. The median NIBR-APG was 4.5 mm Hg (interquartile range, 0.0-10.0 mm Hg). Fifty-six patients (18.4%) exhibited a NIBR-APG greater than 11 mm Hg. Compared with patients without a significant gradient, these patients received higher norepinephrine-equivalent doses (0.23 vs. 0.10 µg/kg/min), had higher Sequential Organ Failure Assessment scores (11 vs. 10), prolonged capillary refill time (3.0 vs. 2.5 s), and higher lactate concentrations (2.7 vs. 1.3 mmol/L). In multivariable analysis, only vasoactive drug dose was independently associated with NIBR-APG greater than 11 mm Hg (odds ratio, 1.68; 95% CI, 1.12-2.52). ICU mortality was higher in patients with significant gradients (48.0% vs. 30.1%).

Conclusions: Nearly one in five critically ill patients receiving vasoactive agents demonstrated a clinically significant NIBR-APG. The presence of this gradient was independently associated with higher vasoactive drug requirements and was accompanied by greater illness severity and higher ICU mortality.

Putowski Z, Gawda R, Czarnik T, Królicki T, Trzebicka J, Zawadka M

item.title: Comparative Analysis of Tracheal Intubation-Associated Cardiac Arrest in 2015-2023: A Report From the National Emergency Airway Registry for Children Multicenter Registry
item.description:
Objectives: To determine the contemporary incidence of tracheal intubation-associated cardiac arrest (TI-CA) in critically ill children and identify potentially modifiable factors to prevent TI-CA in PICUs and pediatric cardiac ICUs (PCICUs).

Design: Retrospective cohort study.

Setting: Seventy international PICUs and PCICUs.

Patients: Critically ill children requiring tracheal intubation in PICUs and PCICUs.

Interventions: Tracheal intubation data were prospectively collected for all initial intubations in 68 PICUs and PCICUs from January 2015 to December 2023 using the National Emergency Airway Registry for Children registry.

Measurements and main results: TI-CA was defined as CA occurrence or receipt of chest compressions for at least 1 minute within 20 minutes of endotracheal tube placement. TI during ongoing cardiopulmonary resuscitation was not considered TI-CA. A total of 27,773 TIs were evaluated, with TI-CA reported in 1.2% (n = 331). Pre-TI oxygenation failure and shock were associated with higher odds of TI-CA (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 2.29; 95% CI, 1.81-2.89 and aOR, 4.67; 95% CI, 3.68-5.92, respectively). Each additional TI attempt required was associated with increased odds of TI-CA (aOR, 1.70; 95% CI, 1.56-1.85, for each attempt). Use of ketamine (aOR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.49-0.82), propofol (aOR, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.27-0.72), neuromuscular blockade (aOR, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.49-0.91), and video laryngoscopy (aOR, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.6-0.97) were associated with lower odds of TI-CA. Mediation analysis indicated that 13% of video laryngoscopy's protective effect was due to a reduction in TI attempt counts. The protective effects of ketamine, propofol, and neuromuscular blockade were minimally mediated by reduced TI attempt counts (5%, 4%, and 7%).

Conclusions: TI-CA occurred in 1.2% of TIs performed in the PICUs. Odds of TI-CA increased incrementally with successive TI attempts. Video laryngoscopy was protective against TI-CA. Mediation analysis revealed that reduced TI attempts accounted for 13% of the protective benefit associated with video laryngoscopy.

Padiyath A, Padiyath F, Berg RA, Napolitano N, Nadkarni V, Shults J

item.title: Scientific Output in Septic Shock According to Country Income and Gender: A Meta-Epidemiological Study
item.description:
Objectives: We aimed to assess trends in septic shock publications by country income and author gender.

Data sources: We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science for articles indexed with "septic shock" between January 2014 and December 2024.

Study selection: All peer-reviewed publication types were eligible. Conference abstracts and non-peer-reviewed material were excluded.

Data extraction: Bibliographic data, first and last author affiliations, country income level (World Bank classification: low- and middle-income countries [LMICs] and high-income countries [HICs]), and journal prestige (SCImago Journal Rank [SJR]) were extracted. Author gender was inferred using the NamSor application programming interface (API).

Data synthesis: Of 10,352 eligible publications, LMIC-affiliated first authors increased over time (+2.13% per year; 95% CI, +1.66 to +2.61; p < 0.001) from 18% in 2014 to 37% in 2024. Women represented 35.6% of first authors and 25.0% of last authors (with around 20% of authors not classifiable by the NamSor API), with higher proportions in LMICs than HICs (p < 0.001) for both first authors (44.5% vs. 32.5%) and last authors (35.2% vs. 21.5%). Gender concordance was more frequent, with female first authors more often paired with female last authors than male first authors (31.7% vs. 21.1%). Cross-income collaborations, especially involving LMIC last authors, remained rare. Articles led by men in HICs were more often published in higher-SJR journals compared with those led by women (p < 0.001), whereas no gender differences were observed among LMIC-affiliated authors.

Conclusions: Despite encouraging growth in LMIC contributions and female representation, major inequities persist. Strengthening equitable collaborations and supporting underrepresented groups would broaden participation and enhance the global applicability in critical care research.

Mora P, Lakbar I, Myatra SN, Gaye B, Ben Souissi A, Hernández G

item.title: Cluster Versus Individual Randomization in Prehospital, Emergency and Critical Care Trials: A Meta-Epidemiological Study
item.description:
Objectives: Cluster-randomized clinical trials (cRCTs) are pooled with individually randomized clinical trials (iRCTs) in meta-analyses. However, cRCTs are associated with methodological characteristics potentially inducing systematic differences compared with iRCTs. In acute settings, trial inclusion is time-sensitive, exacerbating inclusion-based biases. We conducted a meta-epidemiological study to assess deviations in effect estimates between cRCTs and iRCTs in these settings.

Data sources: A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed and Embase.

Data selection: We screened and identified all meta-analyses in prehospital, emergency, or critical care within the last decade that included at least one cRCT and one iRCT.

Data extraction: Data were extracted in duplicate from the meta-analyses. If overlapping trials were identified, results were pooled. The primary outcome was mortality; the secondary outcome comprised length-of-stay- or days-alive-type outcomes.

Data synthesis: Using absolute ln(odds ratio [OR]) for mortality and absolute Hedges' g for the secondary outcome, mean differences (MDs) in effect estimates between cRCTs and iRCTs were analyzed using mixed regression models, presented with 95% CIs. We identified 94 eligible meta-analyses; 44.7% reported on randomization type (cRCT or iRCT). We included 65 meta-analyses in quantitative analyses, encompassing 212 randomized clinical trials (39 cRCTs and 173 iRCTs) and 315,276 patients. No statistically significant difference in absolute ln(OR) for mortality between cRCTs and iRCTs was found (MD, -0.110; 95% CI, -0.093 to 0.313). For length-of-stay- or days-alive-type outcomes, a significant difference in absolute Hedges' g was found (MD, -0.202; 95% CI, -0.392 to -0.012).

Conclusions: A systematic difference between cRCTs and iRCTs in length-of-stay- or days-alive-type outcomes, but not mortality, was identified, with cRCTs reporting smaller effect size magnitudes than iRCTs. With under half of identified meta-analyses reporting on randomization modality, these results highlight the need for improved transparency and statistical consideration of randomization type in future meta-analyses in prehospital, emergency, and critical care.

Lønstrup S, Petersen PL, Bruun NH, Klitgaard TL, Schjørring OL

item.title: Furosemide Stress Test in Adults and Children With Acute Kidney Injury: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
item.description:
Objectives: To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and therapeutic utility of the furosemide stress test (FST) for acute kidney injury (AKI) management in critically ill adults and children.

Data sources: PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from inception to March 3, 2026.

Study selection: Studies evaluating the standardized FST protocol in critically ill adults or children with AKI were eligible. Outcomes included AKI stage 3 progression (Q1), kidney replacement therapy (KRT) initiation (Q2), short-term mortality (Q3), successful KRT liberation (Q4), and FST-guided vs. standard KRT initiation in randomized trials (Q5).

Data extraction: Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed risk of bias using Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 and Risk of Bias 2. Certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework.

Data synthesis: Twenty studies (n = 1979; 11 countries; 2013-2025) were included. For AKI progression (nine studies; n = 501), pooled sensitivity was 0.69 and specificity was 0.88 (area under the curve [AUC], 0.89; GRADE: low). For KRT initiation (nine studies; n = 952), sensitivity was 0.81 and specificity was 0.75 (AUC, 0.79; GRADE: very low). For mortality (six studies; n = 487), sensitivity was 0.56 and specificity was 0.76 (AUC, 0.75; GRADE: very low). For KRT liberation (three studies; n = 177), sensitivity was 0.81 and specificity was 0.87 (AUC, 0.89; GRADE: low for sensitivity, very low for specificity). The effect of FST-guided early KRT initiation on short-term mortality was uncertain (pooled risk ratio, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.79-1.27; two randomized controlled trials, n = 212; GRADE: very low). Pediatric analyses yielded AUC values of 0.81 and 0.63 for KRT initiation and mortality, respectively.

Conclusions: Based on low to very low certainty evidence, the FST may support risk stratification for AKI progression and KRT liberation in critically ill adults. Its impact on mortality when guiding early KRT initiation remains uncertain. As a low-cost bedside test, the FST can be a useful tool in resource-limited settings where novel biomarkers are inaccessible.

Tran PNT, Luong HM, Doan ND

item.title: Ketamine as an Opioid-Sparing Adjunct During Mechanical Ventilation: Feasible and Ready for a Larger Trial
Delay From Hypotension Onset to Appropriate Antifungal Therapy Initiation Is the Critical Determinant of Outcome in Candida Septic Shock
item.description:
Objectives: To determine the effect of delays in initiation of appropriate antifungal therapy from the initial onset of persistent hypotension to the outcome of Candida septic shock.

Design: Retrospective cohort study.

Setting: A total of 32 academic and community hospitals in Canada, the United States, and Saudi Arabia (July 1989 to June 2018).

Patients: A total of 850 adult patients with culture-positive Candida septic shock.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: Out of 850 patients with Candida septic shock, 69.2% patients (589) received appropriate antifungal therapy after the onset of persistent hypotension. A strong relationship was observed between the delay in initiation of pathogen-appropriate antifungal (PAA) therapy and hospital survival. The adjusted odds ratio of death was 1.045 per hour of delay (95% CI, 1.035-1.056; p < 0.0001). The survival rate was 86% when an appropriate antifungal for the isolated pathogen was administered within 2 hours of the initial documentation of persistent hypotension. Thereafter, hospital survival decreased an average of 5.0% per hour for each hour of delay to 10-12 hours of delay. In a multivariate analysis, which included the Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II score and epidemiologic/therapeutic variables, the time to initiation of appropriate antifungal therapy emerged as the single strongest predictor of outcome. Sensitivity analysis further demonstrated that the adverse effects of delayed antifungal treatment were consistent across various subgroups, including different types of infections, pathogens, and antifungal drug classes. Median time to appropriate antifungal therapy was 32.3 hours (interquartile range, 11.2-66.0 hr), with only 16.9% receiving therapy within 6 hours of hypotension onset.

Conclusions: Administration of PAAs within the first hours of documented hypotension significantly improved hospital survival. Less than 20% of patients received appropriate antifungals within 6 hours of documented hypotension.

Abhishek A, Mashhadiagha G, Ramezani A, Wu CP, Wang X, Fan Y

item.title: Music Therapy During Weaning From Invasive Mechanical Ventilation in the ICU: A Randomized Controlled Trial
item.description:
Objectives: The study examined the effect of daily music therapy on weaning from invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) in the ICU, with a primary focus on weaning duration. Secondary agitation, sedation, and analgesia doses, pain, delirium, and perceived stress after 90 days were assessed. Additionally, total IMV and ICU stay durations and tracheostomy rates were studied. Physiologic parameters were assessed in the music therapy group (MG). The study also aimed to promote the humanization of critical care through a biopsychosocial and creative music therapy approach.

Design: Randomized controlled trial with two parallel groups: control group receiving standard care during weaning and MG receiving music therapy additionally.

Setting and patients: Adult critically ill patients (n = 100) admitted to a general ICU who received IMV for at least 48 hours.

Interventions: MG received daily, individualized music therapy sessions averaging 25 minutes, based on patient needs and musical preferences, which included music relaxation, music listening, and clinical improvisation.

Measurements and main results: No significant difference in weaning duration was observed between groups (p = 0.97). Patients in the MG group showed significant improvements in agitation and sedation levels (Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale) on days 1 and 3 (p = 0.048, 0.005, and 0.024) and a lower percentage required propofol (p = 0.028). No significant difference in perceived pain (Visual Analog Pain Scale). The MG obtained lower Perceived Stress Scale-14 scores (p = 0.24). Additionally, MG significantly reduced tracheostomy rates (14%; p = 0.025). Median total IMV and ICU stay duration were shorter in the MG group, but not significantly (p = 0.206 and 0.203). Heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and oxygenation showed no significant difference before and after music therapy.

Conclusions: Music therapy may serve as a nonpharmacological complementary adjunct during weaning by reducing agitation, sedation, and tracheostomy rate. It may potentially decrease perceived stress and IMV and ICU stay durations. Further research is warranted.

Pereiro S, Corral E, Del Campo P, Vallejo A, Argaluza J, Torres E

item.title: Assessment of Tidal Volume in Patients Undergoing Noninvasive Ventilation: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
item.description:
Objectives: Noninvasive ventilation (NIV) is widely used in acute respiratory failure (ARF), yet the association between high tidal volume (Vt) and clinical outcomes remains incompletely defined. We evaluated the association between Vt and NIV failure overall and by ARF type, and its relationship with respiratory and clinical outcomes.

Data sources: MEDLINE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, and Latin American and Caribbean Health Science Literature (1976 to September 2025).

Study selection: Observational studies of adults with ARF treated with NIV reporting Vt or Vt normalized to predicted body weight (Vt/PBW) in NIV success and failure groups.

Data extraction: Three pairs of reviewers identified studies and extracted data independently. Random-effects meta-analysis was performed. Risk of bias and certainty of evidence were assessed using Risk of Bias In Nonrandomized Studies of Interventions and Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation.

Data synthesis: Eleven studies (1136 patients) were included. Vt/PBW was higher in NIV failure vs. success (mean difference [MD], 1.02 mL/kg [95% CI, 0.60-1.45 mL/kg]), whereas absolute Vt did not differ (MD, 1.30 [-33.31 to 35.91]). In hypoxemic ARF, Vt/PBW remained higher in NIV failure (MD, 0.89 mL/kg [95% CI, 0.04-1.73 mL/kg]); no data were available for hypercapnic ARF. Post hoc analyses showed that higher Vt/PBW was associated with increased mortality (odds ratio, 9.11; 95% CI, 3.88-21.37), higher respiratory rate (RR; MD, 3.14 breaths/min [95% CI, 1.36-4.92 breaths/min]), and lower Paco2 (MD, -2.38 mm Hg [95% CI, -4.16 to -0.5938 mm Hg]), but no with pressure support (PS) level (MD, 0.24 [95% CI, -0.81 to 1.29]). Certainty of evidence ranged from very low to moderate.

Conclusions: In adults with ARF treated with NIV, higher Vt/PBW was associated with NIV failure and worse outcomes. These findings reflect prognostic associations rather than causality, and interventional studies with systematic Vt monitoring are needed. Importantly, elevated Vt/PBW, higher RR, lower Paco2, and increased mortality, without differences in PS, collectively implicate elevated respiratory drive as a driver of increased mortality (PROSPERO [CRD42024584977]).Findings: Higher Vt/PBW was associated with NIV failure, particularly in hypoxemic respiratory failure; post hoc analyses showed associations with increased mortality, higher respiratory rate, and lower Paco2.

Santa Cruz R, Matesa A, Jara M, Nadur J, Loudet C, Ricci-Cabello I

item.title: Infections Acquired in the ICU Among Cancer and Other Immunosuppressed Patients: A Nationwide Cohort Study
item.description:
Objectives: To compare the cumulative incidence of ICU-acquired infections (ICU-AIs) across distinct immunosuppression diagnostic categories (solid cancer, hematological cancer, other immunosuppression) and nonimmunosuppressed patients, accounting for competing risks of death and discharge.

Design: Retrospective cohort study using prospectively collected data.

Setting: A total of 50 participating ICUs in Brazil.

Patients: A total of 38,126 adult patients admitted between October 2019 and December 2021 with an ICU stay exceeding 48 hours and no infections diagnosed within the first 48 hours.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: The primary outcome was the incidence of the first ICU-AI during the ICU stay, evaluated using Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard ratios (sHR). In the multivariable competing-risk analysis, patients with hematological malignancies (sHR, 1.64; 95% CI, 1.01-2.65) and other immunosuppressive conditions (sHR, 1.61; 95% CI, 1.02-2.54) were associated with an increased cumulative incidence of ICU-AI, while solid malignancy was not significantly different from non-immunosuppressed patients (sHR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.68-1.14).

Conclusions: Patients with hematological malignancies and other immunosuppressive conditions face a significantly higher risk of ICU-AIs.

Daltro-Oliveira R, Dos Santos SS, Sanches LC, Ferronatto BR, Romano TG, Lisboa TC
